analysis.one_liner: Weakens OSHA workplace safety enforcement by cutting penalties for employers who quickly fix violations.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have reduced OSHA penalties for employers and limited citations on shared worksites, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed how the Occupational Safety and Health Administration enforces workplace safety rules. Employers who fixed a safety violation and certified the fix within 72 hours would owe no penalty for the initial citation, no matter how serious the hazard (except willful violations). On shared worksites like construction projects, only the company whose own workers were exposed to a hazard could be cited — shielding general contractors and other controlling employers. Smaller 'other than serious' citations could no longer be used to build toward higher repeat or willful penalties, and inspectors would have to give employers written notice of all findings and contest procedures at the end of each inspection.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing OSHA inspections. They would pay no fine for an initial citation if they corrected the hazard within 72 hours, get double the time to contest citations (30 workdays instead of 15), and receive a written inspection summary listing every alleged hazard before citations are finalized. Companies that control shared worksites but whose own employees were not exposed would escape citation entirely, and minor citations could no longer escalate into costly repeat or willful penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Secretary of Labor from assessing any penalty on an initial citation — except willful violations — if the employer corrects the hazardous condition and certifies abatement within 72 hours [S2][S3].
On multiemployer worksites, permits OSHA to cite only the employer whose own employees were exposed to the violation, not controlling employers such as general contractors [S2][S3].
Prohibits using 'other than serious' citations as the basis for later repeat or willful citations, capping penalty escalation for employers with prior minor citations [S2][S3].

Doubles the window for employers to contest citations from fifteen to thirty workdays, and requires inspectors to hand employers a written statement at the closing conference listing all alleged hazards, upcoming citations, and contest procedures [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear the cost. The 72-hour fix-and-no-fine rule makes penalties a price employers can avoid after the fact, weakening the financial deterrent to maintaining safe workplaces in the first place. Shielding non-exposing employers on shared sites removes pressure from the general contractors most able to fund safety fixes, and blocking escalation from minor citations removes the accumulated-penalty tool OSHA uses against chronic violators.

drawbacks.text: Forcing inspectors to issue citations within 30 working days (currently 'with reasonable promptness') could mean some complex hazard investigations time out before citations can be issued, letting serious violations go unpenalized [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection in its favor: employers argue OSHA penalties can be crushing for small businesses over paperwork-level violations, and a fix-it-first policy plus clearer written notice at closing conferences is a reasonable due-process improvement [S3].

The cost an honest supporter must acknowledge: the same rules that spare small employers also apply to large, dangerous worksites, and eliminating penalties for initial serious hazards and shielding controlling contractors would lower the cost of unsafe conditions for the employers best positioned to prevent them [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — clearer notice and prompt abatement — is buried inside a package that removes most of the financial consequence of a first citation and shields general contractors on multiemployer sites. The savings for employers are certain and immediate; the cost is a weaker deterrent against the unsafe conditions that cause workplace injuries and deaths. On balance the bill serves regulated employers, not workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, and no action was ever taken on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Todd Tiahrt of Kansas introduced the bill on June 24, 2004, with 18 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on June 24, 2004 [S5].
On July 15, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 without any hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, existing OSHA enforcement — penalties on initial citations, citations of controlling employers on shared worksites, and penalty escalation for repeat violators — stayed in place, and the workers those rules protect are better off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: OSHA enforcement rules and the workers they protect

for.name: 18 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 18 cosponsors were Republicans and none was a Democrat.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 2004 but never reported the bill or held a markup; it then sat in the Workforce Protections Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Republicans with no Democratic support, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral, so no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would erase penalties for initial citations fixed within 72 hours, double the contest window, and require written inspection summaries — reducing the cost and legal risk of a citation for any inspected employer. The savings come directly out of the financial pressure that deters unsafe conditions.

industries.industry: General contractors and controlling employers on multiemployer worksites
industries.note: Under the bill, OSHA could cite only the employer whose own workers were exposed, so companies that control a shared site — the parties most able to finance safety measures — could not be held responsible for hazards affecting other companies' crews. This matters most in construction, where crews from many employers work on one site.

Blocking the use of 'other than serious' citations as the basis for repeat or willful citations protects employers with a history of minor violations from escalating penalties, removing one of OSHA's main tools against chronic violators.
